title: Theoretical Distributions
outcomes: Explain why theoretical probability distributions are useful and distinguish discrete (binomial, Poisson) from continuous (normal) models.
State the conditions and properties of the binomial distribution and compute probabilities, mean, variance and mode.
Use the Poisson distribution, its properties and the Poisson approximation to the binomial.
Apply the properties of the normal distribution and the standard normal table to find probabilities, quartiles and expected frequencies.

meta.exam_tip: MCQs here are mostly property-based: mean np, variance npq, mean = variance = m for Poisson, mean = median = mode for normal, QD = 0.675σ, MD = 0.8σ, inflexion at μ ± σ, and areas 68.27/95.45/99.73%. Learn these cold — each is a 30-second mark.

concepts.title: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
body: A theoretical (probability) distribution spreads the total probability 1 over the possible values of a random variable, the way a frequency distribution spreads total frequency over classes. It lets us predict frequencies, test whether data follow a model and make decisions when observation is costly.

Binomial conditions: (i) a fixed, finite number n of trials; (ii) each trial has only two outcomes — success or failure; (iii) probability of success p is constant (q = 1 − p); (iv) trials are independent.
Probability mass function: P(X = x) = ⁿCₓ pˣ qⁿ⁻ˣ, x = 0, 1, …, n. The probabilities are the successive terms of (q + p)ⁿ and add up to 1. Written X ~ B(n, p).

head: x (invoices with errors)
Formula
P(x)
blocks.title: Binomial probabilities, n = 6, p = 0.1 (first four values)

concepts.analogy: Binomial is a series of n coin tosses with a possibly loaded coin — count the heads.
concepts.work: In attribute sampling an auditor checks n vouchers, each either compliant or not; the number of exceptions follows a binomial model if the error rate is constant.

concepts.title: Properties of the binomial distribution
body: Biparametric: n and p fix the distribution completely.
Mean μ = np; variance σ² = npq; SD = √(npq). Since q < 1, variance < mean. Variance is maximum when p = q = 0.5, and the maximum is n/4.
Mode: if (n + 1)p is not an integer, the mode is its integer part; if (n + 1)p is an integer, the distribution is bimodal with modes (n + 1)p and (n + 1)p − 1.
Symmetric when p = 0.5; positively skewed when p < 0.5 and negatively skewed when p > 0.5.
Additive property: if X ~ B(n₁, p) and Y ~ B(n₂, p) are independent (same p), X + Y ~ B(n₁ + n₂, p).
concepts.analogy: Variance < mean is like a binomial fingerprint — if a question says mean 4 and variance 5, it cannot be binomial.
concepts.work: If 5% of a vendor's invoices are duplicates, out of 200 invoices you expect np = 10 duplicates with SD √9.5 ≈ 3.1 — a quick reasonableness check.

concepts.title: Poisson distribution
body: Uniparametric (only m). Mean = variance = m. Mode: integer part of m if m is not an integer; m and m − 1 (bimodal) if m is an integer.
Poisson approximation to binomial: when n → ∞ and p → 0 such that m = np stays finite (n large, p small, np moderate), B(n, p) ≈ P(m).
Additive property: if X ~ P(m₁) and Y ~ P(m₂) are independent, X + Y ~ P(m₁ + m₂).
Recurrence: P(x + 1) = P(x) × m/(x + 1) — handy for building a table quickly.
concepts.analogy: Poisson counts raindrops landing on one tile in a minute: many chances, each tiny.
concepts.work: Claims per policy, system outages per month and errors per 1,000 transactions are typically modelled as Poisson counts.

concepts.title: Where Poisson applies
body: Use it when the number of opportunities is very large but the chance of the event at each one is very small: printing mistakes per page of a large book; road accidents per minute on a busy road; radioactive emissions per minute; demands per minute at a health centre; defects per metre of cloth.
Binomial needs n and p; Poisson needs only the average rate m — useful when n is unknown or practically unlimited.
concepts.analogy: If you can count how often something happened but not how often it did not, think Poisson.
concepts.work: A bank planning ATM cash or a call centre planning staff uses Poisson arrivals per interval.

concepts.title: Normal distribution
body: The most important continuous distribution: f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] e^(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)), −∞ < x < ∞. Written X ~ N(μ, σ²); biparametric (μ, σ).

Properties: bell-shaped and symmetrical about μ, so mean = median = mode = μ and skewness is zero; unimodal; QD ≈ 0.675σ (Q₁ = μ − 0.675σ, Q₃ = μ + 0.675σ); MD ≈ 0.8σ; points of inflexion at μ − σ and μ + σ; the two tails approach but never touch the x-axis; total area = 1, half on each side of μ.

Areas: P(μ − σ < X < μ + σ) ≈ 0.6827; P(μ − 2σ < X < μ + 2σ) ≈ 0.9545; P(μ − 3σ < X < μ + 3σ) ≈ 0.9973 — almost all values lie within ±3σ. (The ICAI material doubles the half-areas 0.34135 and 0.47725 and prints 0.6828 and 0.9546; the difference is only rounding, and either figure picks out the right option.)
Many distributions tend to normal: binomial when n is large and p not extreme, Poisson when m is large, and sampling distributions of means for large samples.
concepts.analogy: The normal curve is a perfectly balanced hill — the peak, the middle point and the centre of gravity are all at the same spot.
concepts.work: Value-at-risk models, process tolerances (±3σ) and grading on a curve all use normal areas.

concepts.title: Standard normal variate and using the table
body: z = (x − μ)/σ converts any normal variable to the standard normal N(0, 1): mean, median and mode 0; SD 1; MD ≈ 0.8, QD ≈ 0.675; symmetrical about 0; inflexion at z = ±1.
Φ(k) = P(z ≤ k) is read from the table; by symmetry Φ(−k) = 1 − Φ(k). Many exam questions give the area from 0 to k instead; then P(z > k) = 0.5 − area(0, k) and P(−k < z < k) = 2 × area(0, k).
Steps: convert each x to z; sketch the curve and shade the region; combine table areas using symmetry; multiply by N for an expected frequency. For continuous X, P(X ≤ a) = P(X < a).
concepts.analogy: z is a currency converter: whatever the original unit (marks, grams, rupees), it restates the value as "how many SDs from the mean".
concepts.work: A z-score of −2 for a branch's cash variance flags it as unusual (only about 2.3% of branches would be that low if all were normal) — a quick analytical review test.

mcqs.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcqs.q: Which is NOT a condition of the binomial distribution?
options: The probability of success changes from trial to trial
The number of trials is fixed
mcqs.explain: A binomial model needs a fixed number of independent trials, each with two outcomes and the same probability of success p. If p changes from trial to trial, the model breaks, so that is NOT a condition. 'The number of trials is fixed' is the trap: it is a genuine condition. In practice: drawing invoices without replacement from a small batch changes p, so the binomial is only an approximation there.

mcqs.q: For a binomial distribution with n = 20 and p = 0.3, the mean is:
mcqs.explain: The mean of a binomial distribution is np = 20 × 0.3 = 6. The trap is 4.2, which is the variance npq (20 × 0.3 × 0.7), not the mean. In practice: if 30% of 20 sampled invoices are expected to have GST errors, the auditor expects about 6 erroneous invoices on average.

mcqs.q: For a binomial distribution with n = 20 and p = 0.3, the variance is:
mcqs.explain: The variance of a binomial is npq = 20 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 4.2. The trap is 6, which is the mean np. 2.05 is the standard deviation (√4.2). In practice: knowing the spread around the expected number of errors helps an auditor judge whether an observed error count is unusual.

mcqs.q: A binomial distribution has mean 8 and variance 4. The number of trials n is:
mcqs.explain: Variance ÷ mean = npq ÷ np = q, so q = 4 ÷ 8 = 0.5 and p = 0.5. Then n = mean ÷ p = 8 ÷ 0.5 = 16. The trap is 8, which assumes n equals the mean. In practice: working backwards from summary figures to model parameters is common when only reported averages and variances are available.

mcqs.q: A binomial distribution with mean 4 and variance 5 is:
options: Impossible, because the variance of a binomial must be less than its mean
Possible only if n is very large
mcqs.explain: For a binomial, variance = npq and mean = np, so variance ÷ mean = q, which must be less than 1. Here q = 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25, which is impossible. 'Possible with p = 0.8' is the trap: no value of p can make the variance exceed the mean. In practice: checking such internal consistency is how a reviewer spots an error in a statistical report.

mcqs.q: The maximum possible variance of a binomial distribution with n = 12 is:
mcqs.explain: Variance npq is greatest when p = q = 0.5, giving 12 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 3. The trap is 6, which is the mean at p = 0.5, not the variance. In practice: uncertainty is highest when an outcome is a 50–50 call, which is why pollsters plan sample sizes assuming p = 0.5.

mcqs.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcqs.q: Four fair coins are tossed. The probability of exactly two heads is:
mcqs.explain: P(X = 2) = ⁴C₂ × (1/2)² × (1/2)² = 6 × 1/16 = 0.375. The trap is 0.5, the intuitive 'half the coins' guess that ignores the counting. In practice: binomial probabilities like this are used in acceptance sampling to find the chance of a given number of defectives in a sample.

mcqs.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model
mcqs.q: In 5 independent trials with p = 0.4, the probability of no success is:
mcqs.explain: No success means all 5 trials fail: P(0) = q⁵ = 0.6⁵ ≈ 0.0778. The trap is 0.0102, which is p⁵ (all successes). In practice: the probability that a sample contains no errors at all is central to discovery sampling in audit, where finding zero errors supports reliance on a control.

mcqs.q: The mode(s) of B(9, 0.5) is/are:
mcqs.explain: For a binomial, if (n + 1)p is an integer, there are two modes: (n + 1)p and (n + 1)p − 1. Here (9 + 1) × 0.5 = 5, so the modes are 5 and 4. The trap is 4.5, the mean, which is not a possible value of a count. In practice: the most likely number of defectives in a batch guides how quality inspectors set their expectations.

mcqs.q: If X ~ B(5, 0.3) and Y ~ B(7, 0.3) are independent, then X + Y follows:
mcqs.explain: Independent binomials with the same p can be added: n's add, p stays the same. So X + Y ~ B(5 + 7, 0.3) = B(12, 0.3). The trap is B(12, 0.6), which wrongly adds the probabilities. In practice: combining two independent audit samples with the same error rate gives one larger binomial sample, which simplifies evaluation.

mcqs.q: A binomial distribution is symmetrical when:
options: n is large regardless of p
mcqs.explain: A binomial distribution is symmetrical only when p = q = 0.5. If p < 0.5 it is positively skewed, and if p > 0.5 it is negatively skewed. 'n is large regardless of p' is the trap: large n makes it closer to symmetric, but exact symmetry needs p = 0.5. In practice: rare events like defaults (small p) always give right-skewed counts.

mcqs.q: For a Poisson distribution the variance is 3. Its mean is:
mcqs.explain: In a Poisson distribution the mean and variance are equal, both being m. So if the variance is 3, the mean is 3. The trap is 1.73, which is the standard deviation (√3). In practice: if call-centre complaints average 3 per hour, their variance is also 3, a quick check on whether a Poisson model fits.

mcqs.q: For a Poisson variable, P(X = 1) = P(X = 2). The mean is:
mcqs.explain: Set P(1) = P(2): e⁻ᵐ m = e⁻ᵐ m² ÷ 2. Dividing both sides by e⁻ᵐ m gives 1 = m ÷ 2, so m = 2. The trap is 1: that is the mean for which P(0) = P(1), not P(1) = P(2). In practice: fitting a Poisson parameter from observed frequencies is how analysts model arrival rates of customers or claims.

mcqs.q: For a Poisson distribution with mean 4, the standard deviation is:
mcqs.explain: For a Poisson distribution the variance equals the mean, so the variance is 4 and SD = √4 = 2. The trap is 4, which is the variance, not the SD. In practice: if a branch receives on average 4 fraud alerts a week, the typical variation around that is about 2 alerts.

mcqs.q: The mode of a Poisson distribution with m = 3.6 is:
mcqs.explain: When m is not an integer, the Poisson distribution has a single mode equal to the integer part of m. For m = 3.6, the mode is 3. The trap is '3 and 4': two modes occur only when m is an integer. In practice: the most likely number of daily insurance claims is found this way for capacity planning.

mcqs.q: The mode(s) of a Poisson distribution with m = 3 is/are:
mcqs.explain: When m is an integer, the Poisson distribution is bimodal, with modes m and m − 1. For m = 3, the modes are 3 and 2. The trap is '3 only', which forgets that P(2) = P(3) when m = 3. In practice: knowing two counts are equally most likely helps when staffing for customer arrivals.

mcqs.q: For a Poisson variable with m = 2 (e⁻² = 0.1353), P(X ≥ 1) is:
mcqs.explain: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(0) = 1 − e⁻² = 1 − 0.1353 = 0.8647. The trap is 0.1353, which is P(0) itself. In practice: the complement rule gives the chance of at least one event, such as at least one machine breakdown in a shift.

P(X = 2) = e⁻ᵐ mˣ ÷ x! = 0.1353 × 2² ÷ 2! = 0.1353 × 2 = 0.2706. The trap is 0.5412, which forgets to divide by 2!. In practice: Poisson probabilities are used to estimate the chance of a given number of accidents, defects or claims in a period.

mcqs.q: The Poisson distribution is a good approximation to the binomial when:
options: n is large, p is small and np is moderate
n is small and p is large
mcqs.explain: The Poisson approximates the binomial when n is large, p is small and np (the mean) is moderate. 'p = 0.5' is the trap: with p = 0.5, the normal approximation is used instead. In practice: defects in a large production run or errors in a large population of entries are rare events, ideal for the Poisson model.

mcqs.q: If X ~ P(1.5) and Y ~ P(2.5) are independent, the variance of X + Y is:
mcqs.explain: Independent Poisson variables add: X + Y ~ P(1.5 + 2.5) = P(4). For a Poisson, variance = mean, so the variance is 4. The trap is 3.75, which multiplies 1.5 × 2.5 instead of adding. In practice: if two branches independently receive complaints at rates 1.5 and 2.5 per day, total daily complaints follow P(4).

mcqs.q: The number of printing mistakes per page of a large book is best described by:
mcqs.explain: Printing mistakes per page are rare events with many opportunities (every character could be wrong), which is the classic Poisson situation. The normal distribution is the trap: it suits continuous measurements like heights, not small counts of rare events. In practice: Poisson models are used for counting rare events like insurance claims, system failures and fraud alerts.

mcqs.q: For a normal distribution:
mcqs.explain: The normal curve is perfectly symmetrical and has a single peak, so mean, median and mode coincide at μ. 'Mean > median > mode' is the trap: that describes a positively skewed distribution. In practice: when the mean and median of a dataset are far apart, analysts know a normal model may not fit.

mcqs.q: A normal distribution has SD 8. Its quartile deviation is approximately:
mcqs.explain: For a normal distribution, QD ≈ 0.675σ = 0.675 × 8 = 5.4. The trap is 6.4, which is the mean deviation (0.8σ), not the quartile deviation. In practice: these fixed ratios allow quick conversions in risk models where returns are assumed to be roughly normal.

mcqs.q: A normal distribution has SD 15. Its mean deviation is approximately:
mcqs.explain: For a normal distribution, MD ≈ 0.8σ = 0.8 × 15 = 12. The trap is 10.13, which is the quartile deviation (0.675 × 15 = 10.125, rounded). In practice: such ratios help when a report gives only one measure of dispersion and another is needed for comparison.

mcqs.q: The points of inflexion of N(50, 16) are at:
mcqs.explain: In N(μ, σ²), the second figure is the variance, so σ = √16 = 4. The points of inflexion are μ ± σ = 50 ± 4 = 46 and 54. The trap is 34 and 66, which wrongly treats 16 as σ. In practice: misreading variance as standard deviation is a common error when reading risk reports, quadrupling or shrinking the apparent risk.

mcqs.q: In a normal distribution, the percentage of values within μ ± 2σ is about:
mcqs.explain: In a normal distribution, about 68.27% of values lie within μ ± σ, 95.45% within μ ± 2σ and 99.73% within μ ± 3σ. So the answer is 95.45. The trap is 68.27, which is the share within one SD. In practice: Value-at-Risk and quality-control limits in manufacturing are set using these normal coverage figures.

mcqs.topic: Standard normal variate and using the table
mcqs.q: X ~ N(60, 64). The z-value for x = 72 is:
mcqs.explain: N(60, 64) gives σ = √64 = 8. z = (x − μ) ÷ σ = (72 − 60) ÷ 8 = 1.5. The trap is 0.19, which divides 12 by 64, the variance, instead of the SD. In practice: z-scores are used to compare performance on different scales, such as standardising branch sales against the network average.

mcqs.topic: Standard normal variate and using the table
mcqs.q: Given that the area from z = 0 to z = 1 is 0.3413, P(z > 1) is:
mcqs.explain: The area to the right of z = 0 is 0.5. Subtract the area from 0 to 1: P(z > 1) = 0.5 − 0.3413 = 0.1587. The trap is 0.8413, which is P(z < 1), the area to the left. In practice: such tail areas give the chance of an extreme outcome, for example a monthly return worse than one SD below average.

mcqs.q: The two quartiles of a normal distribution are 42.25 and 55.75. Its standard deviation is:
mcqs.explain: For a normal distribution, QD = (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ 2 = (55.75 − 42.25) ÷ 2 = 6.75, and QD ≈ 0.675σ. So σ = 6.75 ÷ 0.675 = 10. The trap is 6.75, which is the QD itself. In practice: recovering σ from quartiles helps when only a range of typical values is published, such as an interquartile salary range.

mcqs.topic: Standard normal variate and using the table
mcqs.q: The standard normal distribution has:
mcqs.explain: The standard normal variate z = (x − μ) ÷ σ always has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. 'Mean 1 and SD 0' is the trap: an SD of 0 would mean no variation at all. In practice: standardising variables to mean 0 and SD 1 is the first step in credit-scoring models and many statistical tools.

mcqs.q: The tails of the normal curve:
options: Approach the x-axis but never touch it
mcqs.explain: The normal curve is asymptotic: its tails get ever closer to the x-axis but never touch it, so any value is possible, however unlikely. 'Touch the x-axis at μ ± 3σ' is the trap: only about 0.27% of values lie beyond, but the curve continues. In practice: this is why risk managers worry about rare 'tail events' in financial markets.

mcqs.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Poisson is uniparametric; binomial and normal are biparametric
mcqs.explain: The Poisson distribution has one parameter (m), so it is uniparametric. The binomial has two (n and p) and the normal has two (μ and σ), so both are biparametric. 'Binomial is uniparametric' is the trap: it needs both n and p. In practice: knowing how many parameters a model needs tells an analyst how much data must be estimated before using it.

viva.q: What are the mean and variance of a binomial distribution, and how do they compare?

viva.q: State the important properties of the normal distribution.
viva.model: The normal curve is bell-shaped and symmetrical about the mean, so the mean, median and mode are equal. It is defined by two parameters, mu and sigma. The quartile deviation is about 0.675 sigma and the mean deviation is about 0.8 sigma. The points of inflexion are at mu minus sigma and mu plus sigma. The two tails never touch the horizontal axis, and the total area under the curve is one.

viva.q: What is the standard normal variate, and what share of values lie within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean?
viva.model: The standard normal variate z equals x minus mu divided by sigma; it has mean zero and standard deviation one. In a normal distribution about 68.27 percent of values lie within mu plus or minus one sigma, about 95.45 percent within two sigma, and about 99.73 percent within three sigma.

viva.q: Give practical situations where the Poisson distribution is used.
viva.model: The Poisson distribution is used for counts of rare events in a large number of opportunities, for example the number of printing mistakes per page of a large book, the number of road accidents per minute on a busy road, the number of calls or demands per minute at a service centre, and the number of defects in a long roll of cloth.

cases.title: Quality control at a bolt factory
cases.case: Kaveri Fasteners makes bolts on an automatic line. On average 2% of bolts are defective, independently of each other. Bolts are packed in boxes of 10, and also shipped in lots of 50 for a customer who rejects a lot if it contains more than one defective. Bolt length is normally distributed with mean 40 mm and SD 0.5 mm; bolts outside 39 mm to 41 mm are scrapped. (Area under the standard normal curve from z = 0 to z = 2 is 0.4772.)

mcqs.q: What is the probability that a box of 10 has no defective bolt?
mcqs.explain: Each bolt is defective with p = 0.02, independently, so a box of 10 is binomial. P(0) = q¹⁰ = 0.98¹⁰ ≈ 0.8171. The trap is 0.1829, which is the probability of at least one defective (1 − 0.8171). In practice: manufacturers quote such figures to customers as the share of defect-free packs.
mcqs.topic: Theoretical distributions and the binomial model

mcqs.q: For a lot of 50 bolts, which approximation is appropriate and what is its parameter?
mcqs.explain: With n = 50 fairly large and p = 0.02 small, B(50, 0.02) is approximated by a Poisson distribution with m = np = 50 × 0.02 = 1. The trap is 'Poisson with m = 2', which uses the percentage 2 directly as the mean. In practice: buyers and suppliers use the Poisson approximation to agree acceptance-sampling plans for large lots.

mcqs.q: Using that approximation, what is the probability that the lot is accepted (at most one defective)?
mcqs.explain: With m = 1, P(0) + P(1) = e⁻¹ + e⁻¹ × 1 = 2e⁻¹ = 2 × 0.3679 ≈ 0.7358. The trap is 0.3679, which is only P(0) and ignores lots with exactly one defective. In practice: this acceptance probability tells the supplier how many of its lots the customer will accept, which feeds directly into pricing and rework costs.

mcqs.q: What proportion of bolts fall within the acceptable length of 39 mm to 41 mm?
mcqs.explain: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ: for 39 mm, z = (39 − 40) ÷ 0.5 = −2; for 41 mm, z = +2. Area = 2 × 0.4772 = 0.9544, so about 4.56% of bolts are scrapped. The trap is 0.4772, which covers only one side of the mean. In practice: manufacturers set tolerance limits in SD terms, the basis of six-sigma quality programmes.
